summary: Discusses architectural implications of Network Address Translation and gives guidelines for implementations. It is informational.

eli5.summary: NAT lets many computers share one Internet address, but it breaks some things. This discusses what and why.

questions: why does nat break the internet
subtitle: Why Network Address Translation breaks the Internet's design principles.

tldr.problem: Network Address Translation (NAT) was deployed widely to address IPv4 address shortage, but it violates the Internet's foundational end-to-end principle where endpoints control communication.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC analyzes the architectural implications of NAT, documenting how NAT devices maintain connection state, break protocol transparency, interfere with security mechanisms, and create operational complexity.
tldr.outcome: NAT became a widespread short-term solution despite its limitations, but at the cost of reduced flexibility, increased complexity, and impediments to deploying IPv6 and security protocols like IPsec.

facts.label: Key concept
facts.value: NAT breaks the Internet's end-to-end principle

today: NAT remains the dominant solution for IPv4 address shortages despite its architectural flaws. IPv6 deployment would eliminate the need for NAT, but the delay caused by NAT's existence means IPv4 and NAT will persist for decades. Understanding NAT's limitations is essential for operating networks, deploying security infrastructure, and planning for IPv6 migration.

sections.title: Why NAT Matters
sections.content:
Network Address Translation (NAT) became popular because it lets many computers share one Internet address, easing the shortage of IPv4 addresses. However, RFC 1631, the original NAT specification, warned that NAT had negative characteristics that made it inappropriate even as a short-term solution. Six years after RFC 1631, this document explains why those concerns remained justified despite NAT's widespread deployment.

The core problem is that NAT violates the Internet's foundational principle: endpoints should control communication, and the network should simply move bits between them. NAT instead puts network devices in the middle, making decisions about connections and modifying packets.
sections.eli5: The Internet was designed so the computers on the ends control talking to each other, and the network just carries messages. NAT puts a gatekeeper in the middle who changes the messages, which breaks how things are supposed to work.

sections.title: How NAT Works and Its Benefits
sections.content:
NAT functions map IP addresses from one network administration to another. The simplest form, Static NAT, provides a one-to-one mapping between private and public addresses. Dynamic NAT maps multiple private addresses to a pool of fewer public addresses, reusing them as connections close. NAPT (Network Address Port Translation), the most common form, multiplexes many private addresses onto a single public address by also translating TCP and UDP ports, letting a whole home or small office network appear as one Internet address.

NAT solves genuine operational problems. It masks address changes when provider connections change or when a company switches ISPs, so internal networks need not be renumbered. It lets ISPs reuse globally routable addresses for intermittent customers, pushing address demand toward the number of active hosts rather than total hosts, extending the IPv4 address space lifetime. NAT also provides an implicit security benefit: inbound connections cannot reach private hosts unless explicitly configured. Application Layer Gateways (ALGs) inspect and modify application data to work around NAT's limitations for applications that embed addresses.
sections.eli5: NAT comes in different varieties. The simple ones swap one address for another. The fancy ones squeeze many internal addresses through one external address. NAT helps when you move providers because only the gateway needs to change. It also squeezes more devices through one Internet address.

sections.title: Architectural Problems NAT Creates
sections.content:
NAT breaks the end-to-end model by requiring network devices to maintain connection state. If a NAT fails, all connections through it fail, and recovery depends on the NAT maintaining consistent, stable storage of its mappings. By contrast, a stateless router failure allows connections to continue through alternate paths.

Many applications embed IP addresses or ports in their payload, assuming the addresses remain valid end-to-end. Examples include FTP (which sends port numbers for data transfers), H.323 (which sends addresses for additional connections), and SNMP (which carries IP addresses in management data). NAT requires an ALG for each such application, and if an application is not anticipated, it fails completely.

IPsec Authentication Headers and Encapsulating Security Payload both protect the IP header itself, so NAT's address changes break authentication. DNS/ALG components that modify DNS responses to work around NAT's namespace fragmentation break DNSSEC. VPN tunnels that cross multiple NATs increase the likelihood of address collisions between independent networks using the same private address ranges. Redundant NATs create complex state synchronization problems and routing asymmetries that are difficult to debug.
sections.eli5: NAT breaks things that depend on the real address. When an app puts an address in its data, NAT can't rewrite it all. Security systems that trust headers get confused. And if the NAT breaks, everything connected through it stops working.

sections.title: Security, IPv6, and Implications
sections.content:
NAT creates an illusion of security without the managed intent of a firewall, leading to false confidence. While applications using TLS, SSL, or SSH can operate transparently through NAT because they do not depend on packet headers, IPsec-based security infrastructure cannot operate end-to-end through NAT. This impediment to deploying network-layer security infrastructure delays broader security adoption.

NAT also complicates IPv6 transition. It extended the IPv4 address space lifetime by a decade or more, reducing the urgency to deploy IPv6 and diverting engineering effort from the long-term solution. During IPv6-to-IPv4 coexistence, NAT can enable widespread IPv6 deployment through 6to4 tunneling, but IPv6-to-IPv4 translation encounters the same architectural problems as IPv4 NAT.
sections.eli5: NAT feels secure but might not be. It stops IPsec from working end-to-end. And because NAT exists, people built more IPv4 stuff instead of moving to IPv6, which would have solved address shortages forever.

sections.title: Deployment Guidelines and Tradeoffs
sections.content:
When deploying NAT, operators must make several critical choices. Static mappings simplify DNS but require manual configuration. Dynamic mappings save address space but require DNS responses to have a TTL of zero so clients do not cache stale addresses. A single NAT creates a clear point of failure, while redundant NATs avoid this but create state synchronization challenges.

Applications that traverse NAT must be examined for address or port dependencies. VPN tunnels must coordinate private address pools to avoid collisions. Secure DNS must either abandon DNSSEC or require DNS/ALG to have access to all source authentication keys. When public services are hosted behind NAPT, only one private host can occupy each well-known port, limiting deployment flexibility.

The core tension is that NAT is a technological diversion needed to sustain IPv4 in the short term, but it undermines the end-to-end principle that made the Internet flexible and powerful. Understanding these tradeoffs is essential for making informed deployment decisions.
sections.eli5: NAT requires careful planning. Choose between easy-but-manual or flexible-but-automated address mapping. Test apps to see if they break. Build redundancy carefully because it is hard to get right. NAT is a short-term fix, not a long-term answer.
